issues.description: Zero-value contract is implicit and enforced only by a reflective test rather than stated in package docs
issues.detail: The PR establishes a real ADT contract (zero/nil receivers return zero values), but it lives only inside a reflection-driven test. The supertype-level promise should be stated in package-level documentation so future accessors honor it by construction, not discovery. Without a written spec, the test approximates the contract instead of proving it.

issues.description: Two parallel nil-zero idioms (`f == nil` vs `IsZero()`) coexist within the same package
issues.detail: *File methods guard with `f == nil` while Type/Member/Oneof/Element guard with `!x.IsZero()`. Mixing both conventions inside one package forces maintainers to remember which type uses which and invites drift. Pick one canonical predicate (e.g. always `IsZero()`, defining `*File.IsZero()` as `f == nil`) so the rule is uniform.

issues.description: The same `var s T; if !zero { s = ... }; return seq.NewFixedSlice(...)` boilerplate is repeated across ~15 accessors
issues.detail: Every getter now opens with the identical defensive five-line ritual instead of pushing nil-tolerance into a helper or into the underlying data structure. One missed guard reintroduces a panic. A single helper (e.g. `zeroSafeSlice` or making `seq.NewFixedSlice` tolerate a zero indexable) would collapse each accessor to one line and eliminate the class.

issues.description: `ValueNodeIndex` returning sentinel `-1` invents a new postcondition that callers will violate
issues.detail: The accessor now returns -1 for the zero element, but the signature is unchanged. Callers doing `e.Value().MessageKeys().At(e.ValueNodeIndex())` will index by -1 and panic, merely relocating the failure. Return `(int, bool)` or expose a `HasValueNode()` predicate so the zero behavior is visible from the signature.

issues.description: Reflection-driven test uses name-based special cases instead of an explicit table
issues.detail: `testZeroAny` walks `reflect.Type.NumMethod`, special-cases `IsZero`, `ValueNodeIndex`, and `Context` by name, and infers accessors from `NumIn==1`. A future method that violates an unstated assumption will fail as a confusing reflect panic, and the `Len()` fallback silently accepts any return type exposing that method. A boring per-type table would be clearer and more durable.

`Imports()` allocates a zero `imports` struct just to dispatch, and `DescriptorProto` on a nil/zero receiver silently returns nil — equivalent to today's behavior but unstated. A caller cannot distinguish "no descriptor.proto available" from "zero file." Document the contract or push nil-tolerance into the receiving types so the dispatch dance disappears.

synthesis.summary: The panel agrees the PR fixes a real class of bug — accessors panicking on zero/nil receivers — and that the reflective zero test is valuable. However, the implementation scatters defensive boilerplate across roughly fifteen accessors rather than capturing the invariant in one helper or in the data structures themselves. The package mixes two nil-zero idioms (`f == nil` vs `IsZero()`), the zero-value contract is stated only in a test rather than in package documentation, and `ValueNodeIndex`'s -1 sentinel quietly invents a new postcondition that callers indexing into `MessageKeys().At` will violate. Intent is sound; shape needs unification before merge.
